appraisal_events.evidence: il n'acceptait jamais qu'Odette vînt le chercher... il aimait mieux passer le commencement de la soirée avec [la jeune ouvrière], étant sûr de voir Odette ensuite; il avait l'impression que personne ne la voyait, ne se mettait entre eux; mais Swann y croyait distinguer maintenant du désenchantement [in the little phrase].
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator lays out Swann's calculated management of timing and access to Odette (delaying his own arrival, refusing to be fetched, guarding the exclusive right to see her home) so that her desire for him will not become sated, giving him quiet control over the relationship's rhythm. This is qualified by the same passage's note that Swann now perceives disenchantment in the little phrase that once symbolized their love, tempering the gain with an undercurrent of doubt.

status_effects.explanation: Swann secures a measure of control and security in the relationship through calculated timing, delay, and exclusivity of access, though the passage's undertone of disenchantment (via the once-joyful little phrase) keeps this from being an unambiguous gain.

ambiguities: The disenchantment Swann perceives in the Vinteuil phrase is filtered through his own subjective impression ('Swann y croyait distinguer'), so it is unclear whether the passage endorses this as genuine foreboding about the affair or merely reports a passing mood in Swann; this affects how strongly the mixed polarity of E1 should be weighted.
